slides.title: Clips, loops, one-shots and the tree
slides.source: Source: Chapter 11, “Ideas you need” and “The Walker example: walker-3d-platformer”; glossary, Animation and interaction.
slides.notes: Clip lengths are from Chapter 11 (idle 1.233 s, walk 1.033 s, run 0.833 s, shooting 0.433 s). Step 3 computes the six leaf weights from five parameters as products down the tree; they sum to 1. The fire time 1.0 s is illustrative.
slides.picture: Four clips with their lengths and a playhead that loops or stops. Then a one-shot shooting clip over a looping run. Then six clip weights computed from five tree parameters.

new_texts: THE CLIPS IN THE ROBOT'S PLAYER
T = 2.50 s run clip time = 0.001 s
A loop wraps: clip time = T mod length.
The player holds the clips and plays one at a time. Idle, walk and run loop; shooting plays once.
all_texts: THE CLIPS IN THE ROBOT'S PLAYER

new_texts: A blend-tree node that plays a clip once over whatever is below it, then returns.
The loop keeps running underneath the whole time.
A OneShot fires a clip once over whatever is below it. When it ends, the loop is all that is left.
all_texts: A blend-tree node that plays a clip once over whatever is below it, then returns.
The loop keeps running underneath the whole time.

new_texts: Godot's graph of blends and state machines.
The tree runs the same clips through a graph. Code writes five numbers; the weights of the six clips follow and sum to 1.

slides.title: Blend tree, blend space and parameters
slides.source: Source: Chapter 11, “BlendSpace: continuous input, continuous pose” and “How its animation is wired”; glossary, Animation and interaction.
slides.notes: MAX_SPEED = 6 is illustrative. The hop uses the trace slope (12.50 falling by about 0.183 per tick). The count of ticks where air_dir is between 0 and 1 comes out near the chapter’s 21.
slides.picture: A stick figure mixed from idle and run by blend_amount. Then three clips on an axis with weights for a moving position. Then three parameter traces over one hop.

new_texts: A graph of nodes that mix clips by numbers your code writes.
commits to one state at a time
ONE BLEND NODE: IDLE MIXED WITH RUN
A blend node mixes two inputs by one number. Idle plus run by speed over MAX_SPEED gives every pose in between.
all_texts: A graph of nodes that mix clips by numbers your code writes.
commits to one state at a time
ONE BLEND NODE: IDLE MIXED WITH RUN
A blend node mixes two inputs by one number. Idle plus run by speed over MAX_SPEED gives every pose in between.

new_texts: Clips placed on a line or a plane; a position between them mixes the nearest ones.
sum = 1.00: only the two nearest clips mix
A blend space puts clips on a line. A position picks the two nearest clips and mixes only those.

new_texts: A tunable number on the tree, addressed by a path; code drives the tree by writing it.
WRITTEN EVERY PHYSICS TICK (120 A SECOND)
air_dir is between 0 and 1 for 22 ticks around the apex.
gun falls below 0.1 after 76 ticks (× 0.97 each).
Code writes the numbers every physics tick. state is 0 or 1 and flips in one tick, with no fade; air_dir and gun move smoothly.

slides.title: State, transition, condition and advance mode
slides.source: Source: Chapter 11, “The state machine, as machinery” and “What we actually ran”; glossary, Animation and interaction.
slides.notes: The six transitions are a sketch: the chapter says five expression transitions plus the added fall to jump. The input rows are scripted, not logged.
slides.picture: Three states, then six transitions, then scripted floor and velocity inputs stepping the machine with the current state highlighted. Then the same input with advance mode Enabled, where nothing fires.

new_texts: One named mode of a state machine, such as idle or run.
how it moves to another state
The machine is in exactly one state: ground.
A state is one named mode. The robot is in ground, jump or fall, never two at once.
all_texts: One named mode of a state machine, such as idle or run.

The machine is in exactly one state: ground.

new_texts: A connection from one state to another, with its own rule for when it fires and how long it blends.
SIX TRANSITIONS (A SKETCH OF CHAPTER 11'S MACHINE)
The five from the chapter, plus the fix: fall to jump.
A transition links two states. Each one has its own rule for when it fires and how long it blends.

slides.title: Travel, priority, interrupt and exit-time
slides.source: Source: Chapter 11, “The state machine, as machinery”; Unity table; glossary, Animation and interaction.
slides.notes: The small machine in step 1 is illustrative. Step 3 and 4 use the run clip length 0.833 s and a request at 0.3 s (illustrative).
slides.picture: A small state graph with a dot travelling along the shortest path. Then three transitions with priorities. Then a clip timeline cut off by an immediate transition, and the same clip waited out by an exit-time transition.

new_texts: Ask the machine to go to a state by the shortest path of transitions; with no path it jumps there.
waits for the clip to end
TRAVEL() ON A SMALL ILLUSTRATIVE MACHINE
travel("run") from idle: idle → walk → run, 2 hops
travel("swim"): no path, so the machine jumps there.
travel() finds the shortest path with A*. The dot walks it. If no path exists, the machine just jumps to the target.

new_texts: Which transition wins when several are true at once; in Godot the lower number is preferred.
THREE TRANSITIONS OUT OF RUN, ALL CHECKED THIS TICK
Two are true. The lower number wins: run → jump.
Several transitions can be true at once. Godot takes the one with the lowest priority number.

slides.title: Cross-fade, transition time and the current node
slides.source: Source: Chapter 11, “The state machine, as machinery”, and the landing trace; glossary, Animation and interaction.
slides.notes: Weights are linear in this sketch; Godot also has an easing curve (xfade_curve). Frame counts are ceil(time × 60). The chapter’s trace: the machine reports the new current node as soon as the fade begins.
slides.picture: Two weight lines over 0.1 seconds that always sum to one. Then transition times of 0, 0.05 and 0.1 seconds with frame counts at 60 frames a second. Then the reported current node against the real weights.

new_texts: Blend smoothly from one clip to the next over a short time.
switch in one tick, no blend
WEIGHT OVER TIME (S), TRANSITION TIME 0.10 S
The two weights always add up to 1.
A cross-fade moves weight from the old state to the new over the transition time. The two weights add up to 1.
all_texts: Blend smoothly from one clip to the next over a short time.
switch in one tick, no blend
WEIGHT OVER TIME (S), TRANSITION TIME 0.10 S
The two weights always add up to 1.
A cross-fade moves weight from the old state to the new over the transition time. The two weights add up to 1.

new_texts: WEIGHT OF THE NEW STATE FOR THREE TRANSITION TIMES
xfade 0.00 s: a cut, one tick
xfade 0 is a cut. 0.05 s is 3 frames at 60 fps; 0.1 s is 6. Count frames before choosing seconds.
all_texts: Blend smoothly from one clip to the next over a short time.
switch in one tick, no blend
WEIGHT OF THE NEW STATE FOR THREE TRANSITION TIMES
xfade 0.00 s: a cut, one tick
xfade 0 is a cut. 0.05 s is 3 frames at 60 fps; 0.1 s is 6. Count frames before choosing seconds.

new_texts: The playback's reading of the current state. During a cross-fade it already names the new state.
WHAT get_current_node() REPORTS DURING THE FADE
At 0.05 s the new state has only half the weight, yet the playback already reports it as current. Read the fading-from node too.

slides.title: Property tracks, method tracks and tweens
slides.source: Source: Chapter 10, “The AnimationPlayer and its tracks” and “Tween or AnimationPlayer”; glossary, Animation and interaction.
slides.notes: Keys are from the sword’s attack_fast clip in Chapter 10: rotation −80, 85, 75 at 0, 0.15, 0.2 s; method keys at 0.1 and 0.25 s; the monitoring key times 0 and 0.15 s are the Chapter 10 pin. The kill time 0.07 s is illustrative.
slides.picture: The sword's attack clip with rotation and monitoring keys and a playhead. Then method keys firing at 0.1 and 0.25 seconds. Then a tween that is killed at 0.07 seconds leaving the hitbox flag on, beside a clip key that turns it off at 0.15 seconds.

new_texts: A track that animates any property, not just bones.
A property track keys any property: the blade's rotation, or monitoring on the hitbox. Each key is a number in the clip.
all_texts: A track that animates any property, not just bones.
A property track keys any property: the blade's rotation, or monitoring on the hitbox. Each key is a number in the clip.

new_texts: Unity: Animation Event. Unreal: Anim Notify
A track that calls a function when the playhead reaches a key.
A method track calls a function when the playhead crosses a key. The editor does not fire it when you scrub.

new_texts: Code-made animation of a value toward a target, then discarded; it can be killed halfway.
WHO TURNS THE HITBOX OFF? (TIME IN S)
The off call lived inside the dead tween, so it never runs.
A tween is made in code. Kill it halfway and the end of its job never happens. Keep gameplay facts on the clip.

slides.title: Sampling and the intermittent fault
slides.source: Source: Chapter 11, “Where the timing gaps come from” and “The question”; glossary, Animation and interaction.
slides.notes: Tick values follow the chapter’s trace (12.50, 12.32, 12.14). The two landing cases are the two tick offsets the chapter’s test pins. Machine states are computed with the five-transition machine, before the fix.
slides.picture: Eight physics ticks around a landing, grouped two to a rendered frame, with the machine state the tree reaches at the end of each frame. Two landing cases: one where the landing is seen, one where it is missed.

new_texts: Reading a value at one moment, so brief events between samples can be missed.
LANDING ON THE FIRST TICK OF A FRAME
120 ticks ÷ 60 frames = 2 ticks per frame; the tree sees one.
Physics runs 120 ticks a second; the tree updates 60 times. It only sees the state at the end of each frame.
all_texts: Reading a value at one moment, so brief events between samples can be missed.
LANDING ON THE FIRST TICK OF A FRAME
120 ticks ÷ 60 frames = 2 ticks per frame; the tree sees one.
Physics runs 120 ticks a second; the tree updates 60 times. It only sees the state at the end of each frame.

new_texts: A bug that appears only sometimes.
Case 1: still fall while rising. Case 2: jump.
Same key held, two outcomes: it depends on tick timing.
LANDING ON THE SECOND TICK OF A FRAME
Land on the first tick and the next tick takes off: the tree never saw the floor and the robot rises in its falling pose.

slides.title: What a probe shows, and a mutation check
slides.source: Source: Chapter 11, “What its checks establish”, “What remains unverified”, “Mutation check”.
slides.notes: The four assertions and the six unchecked items are quoted in substance from the chapter’s “What remains unverified”. Pass and fail cells in step 3 are computed from the sampling simulation. The chapter saw the pre-fix scene fail at both offsets over three hops.
slides.picture: Four probe assertions passing with and without the animation tree. Then six things the probe never checked. Then a state test failing on the pre-fix scene for one landing case but passing on the fixed scene.

new_texts: A script that loads the real scene, presses only ordinary actions and records what happens.
4 of 4 pass with the tree; 4 of 4 pass with it deleted.
Each assertion reads the body, never the pose.
The probe loads the real scene and presses only ordinary actions. It passes all four assertions with the animation tree deleted.
all_texts: A script that loads the real scene, presses only ordinary actions and records what happens.
4 of 4 pass with the tree; 4 of 4 pass with it deleted.
Each assertion reads the body, never the pose.

new_texts: THE PROBE'S OWN LIST OF WHAT IT DID NOT CHECK
Animation is not on the list either: nothing checks it.
It also did not check coins, enemies, the camera image, audio, real controls, or fun. Those need a person.

new_texts: Put the old broken version back and run the new test; it must fail.
STATE TEST ON TWO SCENES, BY LANDING TICK
A test that fails on the old scene is a test that can see the bug.
Run at one landing only, it could pass by luck.
Put the old scene back. The new test must fail there. At the lucky landing alone it passes anyway.

slides.title: Before you trust an animation change
slides.picture: A checklist of six items drawn one at a time.

new_texts: Is the machine pulled by expressions or pushed by travel(), and how often does the tree look?
Can every transition fire: advance mode Auto, or a travel() that uses it?
Is each state reachable and able to exit, with one owner of the state?
Is each cross-fade written in seconds, and how many frames is that?
Does the hitbox window live on the clip, pinned by a frame-stepped check?
What did the test not see: feel, look, fun? Say what you checked.
Then say it exactly: not “make it smoother”, but “0.1 s cross-fade, tested at both landings”.
